lesson.title: Lesson 1: Introduction to Fractions and Equal Parts
lesson.subject: Mathematics

timeFit.suggestion: This lesson runs about 8 min over 40 min. Nothing was removed. Suggestion: move the activity to homework or shorten it to a 5-minute pair task.

data.text: Welcome to our new chapter on fractions! Imagine Meena sitting down for a meal and cutting one round roti into 4 equal parts. When she eats one of those parts, she has eaten a specific fraction of the whole roti called one-fourth. Fractions are all around us in our daily life, helping us describe parts of a whole thing.

blocks.narration: Welcome, class! Have you ever shared a roti, a chapati, or a pizza with your friends by cutting it into equal pieces? Let us find out how we name those pieces using fractions.

data.heading: Parts of a Roti
paragraphs: Think of a warm roti cut into equal pieces. The bottom number tells us the total number of equal parts.
The top number tells us how many parts we are taking to eat or share.

blocks.narration: Think of a roti cut into equal pieces. The bottom number tells us the total number of equal parts, and the top number tells us how many parts we are taking.

data.title: Paper Folding Activity: Making Fourths
instructions: Take your square sheet of paper and fold it neatly in half from top to bottom.
Fold it in half again from left to right so that you form a smaller square.
Unfold the paper completely and look at the four smaller squares you have created. Each small square is exactly one-fourth, or 1/4, of the whole paper.

blocks.narration: Let's take a square sheet of paper and fold it twice to create four equal squares, showing how each part is one-fourth of the whole.

data.heading: Watch Out for Equal Parts!
paragraphs: Always remember that a fraction is only correct when all the parts are truly equal in size. If a chapati is torn into two uneven pieces, the smaller piece is not a real half.
Half means both pieces are exactly the same size. Keep this in mind whenever you divide shapes or food into fractions!

blocks.narration: Always make sure your parts are equal! A torn chapati with uneven pieces does not make a true half.

data.question: Where do the four equal hops from 0 to 1 land on the number line?

blocks.narration: Every fraction has a place on the number line. Let's draw a line from 0 to 1 and divide the gap into 4 equal hops to find our fourths.

points: Watch out for common student mix-ups where children forget that fraction parts must always be equal in size.
Help students who compare denominators incorrectly by taking things slowly with concrete paper-folding exercises.
Use picture-first methods and number lines together to clearly fix these misconceptions before moving ahead.

blocks.narration: Let's take our time with paper folding and number lines today so every student truly sees why equal parts and denominators matter so much.

questions: Why must all parts of a whole be equal when we talk about fractions?
If a roti is cut into 4 equal parts and Meena eats 3 parts, what fraction has she eaten?
In the fraction 3/4, what does the number 4 (the denominator) tell us?

blocks.narration: Let's check what we have learned today about equal parts and fractions before we finish our lesson.

verifiedLesson.title: Lesson 2: Equivalent Fractions and Fractions of a Collection
verifiedLesson.subject: Mathematics

timeFit.suggestion: This lesson runs about 8 min over 40 min. Nothing was removed. Suggestion: move the activity to homework or shorten it to a 5-minute pair task.

data.text: Welcome, class! We use fractions all day in our daily lives without even realizing it. Whether it is pouring half a glass of milk, looking at the clock, weighing half a kilogram of sugar, or sharing one-third of a pizza, fractions are all around us.

blocks.narration: Welcome, everyone! Take a moment to think about your day. Have you ever poured half a glass of milk or shared one-third of a pizza? Let us discover how fractions appear everywhere in our daily lives.

data.heading: Exploring Equivalent Fractions
paragraphs: Fractions that name the same amount are called equivalent fractions. For example, 1/2, 2/4, and 4/8 all represent the exact same portion of a whole.
We can find these friendly fractions by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the same number. When we multiply the top and bottom of 1/2 by 2, we get 2/4.
If you check this on a paper strip, you will see that 1/2 and 2/4 cover the exact same length. Isn't it wonderful how different numbers can describe the very same amount?

blocks.narration: Fractions that name the same amount are called equivalent fractions. We can find them by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the same number!

data.caption: On a paper strip, 1/2 and 2/4 cover exactly the same length.

blocks.narration: Let us look at our paper strip visual to see that one-half and two-fourths cover the exact same length.

data.heading: Fractions of a Collection
paragraphs: Fractions do not just work on single shapes; they also work on groups of things like collections of objects. If you have 12 marbles and want to find one-third of them, you first make 3 equal groups of 4 marbles each.
Once the collection is divided into equal groups, you take just one of those groups. This shows us that taking 1/3 of 12 gives us 4 marbles.
We can use this exact same grouping method for other amounts too. For example, finding 1/4 of 12 gives us 3, and taking 3/4 of 12 gives us 9.

blocks.narration: Let's learn how fractions work with groups of items, like finding one-third of a collection of marbles by sorting them into equal groups.

data.title: Finding Fractions of a Collection
materials: Paper and colored pencils for drawing
instructions: Take 12 counters and arrange them in a straight line on your desk. To find 1/4 of 12, divide your counters into 4 equal groups. Count how many counters are in one group to find your answer.
Next, use your 12 counters to find 3/4 of 12. First make 4 equal groups, and then count how many counters are in 3 of those groups combined.
Draw your counters on a piece of paper to show your work for both problems and share your method with a partner.

blocks.narration: Let's use our counters to find fractions of a collection. Watch how we split twelve items into equal groups to solve problems like one-fourth and three-fourths of twelve.

points: Keep a close eye out for students who forget that all parts of a fraction must be completely equal in size.
Watch out for children who compare denominators incorrectly, such as guessing that 1/6 is bigger than 1/3 simply because 6 is bigger than 3.
Use slow, picture-first work with paper folding and number lines to gently guide students past these common pitfalls.

blocks.narration: Let's remember to watch out for common traps today, like uneven parts or misjudging denominators, and use paper folding to help students see the truth.

questions: Why must all parts of a shape be equal when we talk about fractions?
If you have 12 marbles and you want to find 1/4 of them, how many marbles will you take?
Which fraction is bigger: 1/3 or 1/6? Explain why using the example of cutting a laddoo.

blocks.narration: Great job today, everyone! Please take a moment to answer these three exit ticket questions on your slate or paper before you pack up.
